text: Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings. Substrings are contiguous, and different start and end positions count separately, even if the text is the same.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — so a-a-a counts as six, not three, because the three single a's, the two a-a's, and the one a-a-a are all distinct by position?
Exactly right — six. Length up to about a thousand.
Let me confirm one more. A-b-c has just the three single letters and no longer palindrome, so three. Good.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of interval DP, because a palindrome with both ends peeled off is still a palindrome — a recurrence over ranges. So dp of i, j means s from i to j is a palindrome. The trick is that every true cell is exactly one palindromic substring, so I just count true cells. There's also expand-around-center with constant space.

Here's the plan. One: every single character is a true cell, and so is every pair of matching neighbors — count each. Two: for length three and up, a range is true when its ends match and its inside is true; count it. Three: fill by length, ascending, and return the count. One thing worth flagging — the count equals the number of true cells, because each palindrome maps to a unique start and end pair. No dedup needed. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code the DP and the expand version.

Alright, let me code this up. The interval DP is the longest-palindrome table, but counting: each base loop and each true transition does res plus plus. Then expand-around-center — constant space, counting as you expand. Every index is an odd center and, with its right neighbor, an even center; count grows outward while the ends match. Both are quadratic time. One thing worth flagging — each successful expansion step is one more palindrome, so count just tallies steps. And I need both odd and even centers, to catch a-type and b-b-type palindromes.

Let's dry-run the DP on a-a-a, expected six. Length one gives three true cells; length two adds both a-a's, so five. The row that matters is length three: the outer a's match and the middle a is already true, so the whole string counts — six. That matches. Cross-check with expand: the centers contribute one, one, two, one, one and zero — also six. And a-b-a gives four: three singles plus a-b-a itself. Correct.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is quadratic for both. Space is quadratic for the DP table, constant for expand-around-center. Oh, one more thing — this is literally the longest-palindrome table with the finishing move swapped: track-longest becomes count. The same dp table also works as a constant-time is-this-slice-a-palindrome oracle when partitioning a string into palindromes. And for n up to ten to the fifth, Manacher's algorithm counts in linear time — the count is the sum of the palindrome radii.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that the count equals the number of true cells, with a clean one-to-one argument. You gave both odd and even centers in the constant-space version. And you tied it back to the longest-palindrome table, to palindrome partitioning, and to Manacher. Good work.
